title: The Case For SMCI Stock Survives One Real Flaw
detail:
The Case For SMCI Stock Survives One Real Flaw
Trefis Team
Thu, August 13, 2026 at 7:10 AM PDT 4 min read
HPE
NTAP
ANET
SMCIP
CSCO
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Photo by geralt on Pixabay

After a steep sell-off, a key AI infrastructure builder looks cheap, but the market is pricing in a flaw that bargain hunters cannot afford to ignore.

Super Micro Computer (SMCI) builds the high-performance servers and storage systems that are the backbone of the AI revolution. Yet for a company at the center of a historic technology buildout, its stock tells a conflicting story. After a year in which it underperformed the S&P 500, the stock now trades at just 16.5 times earnings, a sharp discount to the market median of 23.6. Is that discount a gift from a skittish market, or is it an honest verdict on a deteriorating business?

Does the growth story justify the discount?

The value case is overwhelming. Super Micro's revenue grew 56% over the last twelve months, still strong, even if below its 73% three-year average growth rate. Far from being a historical artifact, this remains a business scaling rapidly; management just reported receiving "over $60 billion in new orders" in a single quarter, building on prior-quarter orders, driving its backlog to record levels. The company is so confident in this demand that it is guiding for full-year revenue in fiscal 2027 to land between $65 billion and $72 billion.

The strategy extends beyond a simple volume play. Management is making a strategic push into higher-value, integrated systems it calls Data Center Building Block Solutions, or DCBBS. The goal is to become a one-stop shop for data center construction, a move intended to build a more profitable and defensible business. This strategy is critical, as a company's valuation often hinges on the quality of its earnings, not just the quantity.

So why did a huge margin beat spook the market?

The clearest flaw in the numbers: full-year gross margin slipped from 11.1% to 10.8% year-over-year, a small decline, but one that sits awkwardly next to the revenue growth story. This single data point gets to the heart of the market's skepticism, which is rooted in the business story behind the numbers. In its most recent quarter, the company reported a non-GAAP gross margin of 17.6%, a figure that demolished its own guidance. But in the same breath, it guided the next quarter's margin down to a range of 10.4% to 10.8%.

That volatility is the entire bear case. Management explained that the margin beat was largely due to a favorable product mix, which included the deferral of some lower-margin contracts into the next quarter. This, combined with revenue that landed at the low end of guidance because of "delays in customer readiness," paints a picture of a business struggling with the execution risks of rapid scaling. For investors, it raises the question of whether profitability is truly improving or just unpredictable. For some, a falling multiple on a key ecosystem partner like NVIDIA is a warning, not a bargain, and they may see similar risks here.

title: Super Micro Guided Fiscal 2027 Revenue $16 Billion Above Wall Street and Missed the Quarter Anyway
detail:
Super Micro Guided Fiscal 2027 Revenue $16 Billion Above Wall Street and Missed the Quarter Anyway
Daniel Sparks, The Motley Fool
Wed, August 12, 2026 at 8:39 PM PDT 5 min read
SMCI
NVDA
LSEG.L
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Super Micro Computer (NASDAQ: SMCI) reported its fiscal fourth-quarter results (for the period ended June 30) after the market closed on Tuesday. Revenue of $11.1 billion came in below the $11.55 billion analysts polled by LSEG were expecting.

But the stock rose anyway, gaining about 7% in Tuesday's extended session and about 19% on Wednesday as of this writing.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

The reason is the outlook. For fiscal 2027, management guided revenue to a range of $65 billion to $72 billion. Analysts were modeling about $52.5 billion, according to LSEG. In other words, the artificial intelligence (AI) server maker just guided $16 billion above what Wall Street had penciled in, measured at the midpoint of the range.

Image source: The Motley Fool.
The margin changed the quarter

The quarter itself was hardly weak. Revenue rose 93% year over year, from $5.8 billion in the year-ago quarter, and was up from $10.2 billion in fiscal Q3.

That brought fiscal 2026 revenue to $39.1 billion, up 78% from $22.0 billion in fiscal 2025.

The quarter's standout figure, however, was gross margin. Supermicro posted a 17.5% gross margin, up from 9.9% in fiscal Q3 and 9.5% in the year-ago period. That's above even the preliminary 15% to 17% range the company flagged in its July 21 business update. For context, management originally guided the quarter to a gross margin of just 8.2% to 8.4%.

That swing turned a modest revenue quarter into an enormous profit quarter. Net income came in at $1,178 million, up about sixfold from $195 million a year earlier. Management attributes the margin jump primarily to a richer mix of enterprise customers and broader adoption of its Data Center Building Block Solutions architecture.

Worth remembering: these results are preliminary, as the company's financial closing procedures for the year aren't complete. And Supermicro's board is still conducting an independent review of certain transactions tied to alleged export-control issues. The company itself notes the outcome could affect its forecasts.

What $65 billion needs

A fiscal 2027 revenue range of $65 billion to $72 billion implies growth of 66% at the low end and 84% at the high end. Two things have to hold for that to happen.

The first is the order book converting. Supermicro received more than $60 billion of new orders in the fourth quarter alone, pushing its backlog to record levels entering fiscal 2027. So the guide has real order support behind it. Of course, orders can slip or shrink before they become revenue, and the company has noted some of those commitments may not be firm.

The Dow lagged as traders priced in limited traffic through the Strait of Hormuz and stalled peace talks. To a large extent, another strong earnings season has offset uncertainty about high energy prices and geopolitical tensions — Bloomberg analysis shows that so far, over 85% of companies have beaten analyst expectations. However, some analysts warn that these highs may not last and advise caution.

In July, the consumer price index aligned with forecasts, as monthly headline inflation rose 0.1%, bringing the year-over-year rate to 3.4%. Core CPI, which excludes volatile energy and food components, increased 0.2% for the month and 2.5% compared to the prior year. Both core and headline annual metrics reflected a marginal slowdown relative to June's figures.

Inflation concerns have had a grip on investor sentiment over the past few trading sessions, especially after three officials dissented on July 29 in favor of raising rates.

"The big surprise with a report that had no surprises is that a situation where inflation isn't reaccelerating, coupled with the most recent, weak jobs report gives the Fed more time to wait," Chris Zaccarelli at Northlight Asset Management told Bloomberg.

The next Federal Reserve rate announcement meeting is due in September, and there is another inflation release scheduled before the central bank meets.

While prices remain elevated, the latest CPI should give investors greater confidence that peak inflation appears to be behind us, according to Bret Kenwell at eToro.
